member.name: T:ExpControlsLib.ClvDropWrapper
member.summary: The ClvDropWrapper class deals with the mechanics of receiving a Drag/Drop operation for a ListView. In effect, it implements the IDropTarget interface for a ListView. It is designed to handle a ListView which must have CShItems in the Tags of the ListViewItems contained in the control. The ListView must also have the CShellItem of the single Parent Folder stored in its' .Tag Property
member.remarks:
The class receives the DragEnter, DragLeave, DragOver, and DragDrop events for the associated ListView and performs the Drag specific processing. Unlike CtvDropWrapper, this class DOES NOT raise ShDragxxx events for the ListView, and DOES do the GUI related processing.
The interesting part of this class is that it makes no decisions about the drag nor does any Drop related processing itself. Instead, it acts as a broker between the Drag/Drop operation and the IDropTarget interface of the underlying Shell Folder. This allows the Shell Folder, which may be a Shell Extension, to perform whatever action it needs to in order to effect the Drag/Drop. The benefit of this approach is that Drag/Drop targets need not be part of the File System. ListViews, unlike TreeViews, may be displaying non-folder items and may have substantial areas within the control that are empty of any ListViewItems. This requires different behavior rules for a ListView receiving a Drag.
Upon DragEnter, the "parent" directory of the entire set of Listview items is determined. The "parent" is determined from the CShItems contained in the ListViewItem.Tags or if there are no ListViewItems, from the CShellItem contained in the ListView's .Tag.
The default pdweffect for this control/drag is obtained from the IDropTarget of that "parent"
If there is no common "parent" and if the ListView's Tag does not contain a CShellItem, the default pdweffect for this control/drag is set to "None"
Upon DragOver:
If over a ListViewItem representing a Directory,Obtain IDropTarget from the Directory, and invoke its DragEnter,DragOver to set pwdeffects.
Also set BackGroundColor of that ListView Item to SelectedColor
If not over a ListViewItem representing a directory AndAlso a common "parent" can be determined from the ListViewItems or the ListView's .Tag Property then use IDropTarget of parent to accept DragOver and adjust pdweffect.
If not over a ListViewItem representing a directory AndAlso if no common "parent" can be determined, then set pwdeffects to "None"
Upon DragLeave, all local vars are reset to "New" state
Upon DragDrop, the IDropTarget.DragDrop of the Folder represented by the current ListViewItem is called and all local vars are reset to "New" state.

member.summary: Thread-static bridge that lets an in-app implementation (CtvDropWrapper / ClvDropWrapper) report the resolved destination shell item back to the drag source () before returns on the same STA thread.

remarks.para: OLE DoDragDrop runs a modal message loop on the STA thread that started the drag. Any in-process drop handler that participates in that drag runs its IDropTarget.DragDrop on that same thread before DoDragDrop returns. This makes a single slot sufficient to carry the destination from the drop side back to the source side — no marshaling, no races. The slot is single-use: clears it before each drag and consumes it immediately after DoDragDrop returns.

The slot also carries the [] being dragged (the source items), recorded by before DoDragDrop starts and peekable (non-consuming) by an in-app drop target such as while the drop is in progress. This lets a tree-target drop raise a DragCompleted-style event that includes both the destination and the source items without a separate correlation channel.

External drops (Explorer, desktop) never enter an in-process drop handler, so the slot remains empty and reports no destination — callers fall back to the existing shell change-notification path for moves.
This type is ; it is an implementation detail of the drag-and-drop plumbing and not part of the public surface.

member.name: M:ExpControlsLib.ExpTree.MakeNode(WindowsApiLib.Shell.CShellItem)
member.summary:
Creates a TreeNode whose .Text is the DisplayName of the CShellItem.
Sets the IconIndexes for that TreeNode from the CShellItem.
Sets the Tag of the TreeNode to the CShellItem
If the CShellItem (a Folder) has or may have sub-Folders (see Remarks), adds a Dummy node to the TreeNode's .Nodes collection. This is always done if the input CShellItem represents a Removable device. Checking further on such devices may cause unacceptable delays. Returns the complete TreeNode.
member.param: The CShellItem to make a TreeNode to represent.
member.returns: A TreeNode set up to represent the CShellItem.
member.remarks:
This routine will not be called if the CShellItem (a Folder) is Hidden and ExpTree's ShowHidden Property is False.
If the Folder is Hidden and ShowHidden is True, then this routine will be called.
If the Folder is Hidden and it only contains Hidden Folders (files are not considered here), then, the HasSubFolders attribute may be returned False even though Hidden Folders exist. In that case, we must make an extra check to ensure that the TreeNode is expandable.
There are additional complication with HasSubFolders.
On XP and earlier systems, HasSubFolders was always returned True if the Folder was on a Remote system. On Vista and above, the OS would check and return an accurate value. This extra check can take a long time on Remote systems - approximately the same amount of time as checking item.GetDirectories.Count. Versions 2.12 and above of ExpTreeLib have a modified HasSubFolders Property which will always return True if the Folder is on a Remote system, restoring XP behavior.
On XP and earlier systems, compressed files (.zip, .cab, etc) were treated as files. On Vista and above, they are treated as Folders. ExpTreeLib continues to treat such files as files. The HasSubfolder attribute will report a Folder which contains only compressed files as True. In MakeNode, I simply accept the Vista and above interpretation, setting a dummy node in such a Folder. An attempt to expand such a TreeNode will just turn off the expansion marker.

member.name: T:ExpControlsLib.LVColSorter
member.summary: LVColSorter is ListView in non-virtual mode to sort items. (not used in virtual mode) LVColSorter may be used as the ListViewItemSorter for ListViews populated by any means, but works best when the .Tag properties of the ListViewItems and SubItems are set as described in Remarks.
member.remarks:
LVColSorter uses the .Tag properties of ListViewItems and SubItems to Sort the contents of a ListView based on the underlying data. If no .Tag properties are set, or if the value of those properties do not implement the IComparable interface, then LVColSorter sorts based on the .Text properties of the SubItems of the ListViewItems.
If the .Text properties of SubItems are structured properly for Sorting, then no .Tag information is required for Sorting. Most .Text is not properly structured for Sorting. In that case, the .Tag property may be set to provide this class with the information needed for a proper Sort.
Set the .Tags as follows:
Each ListViewItem The Class instance or DataRow from which the ListViewItem is built. The instance should support the IComparable Interface, if not, it is ignored for Sort purposes and may be omitted.
Each SubItem If the .Text property will not Sort correctly, then the .Tag should be set to the original Value (Date, Double, etc.) See the documentation of the Compare Method of this Class for the actual Sort rules.
Class Properties or DataRow Fields whose Value is a String will Sort based on that String. String Properties that have been Formatted in a non-Sortable Format in the original data will not Sort correctly. The application will have to deal with that case separately by setting the SubItem.Tags to a Sortable Value.
Each instance of LVColSorter will handle the ListView.ColumnClick event for the associated ListView. The using application should not Handle that Event. When a new ListViewItemSorter is assigned to a ListView, any prior instances of LVColSorter will remove themselves from the EventHandler list of that ListView. In other words, multiple ListViewItemSorters may be assigned to a ListView without causing prior instances to attempt to handle ColumnClick.

Odd numbers of clicks on a column will sort Ascending, even numbers will sort Descending (click 1 Ascending, Click 2 Descending ...). The Sort rules are:
If the Clicked column is Column 0 and the ListViewItem's Tag supports the Icomparable Interface, then Compare the ListViewItems Tags.
Otherwise, or if the ListViewItems .Tags Compare Equal, then continue with the following rules.
If the Clicked column's ListViewItem.SubItem's Tag property supports the IComparable Interface, then use CompareTo to compare the .Tags
If the Clicked column's ListViewItem.SubItem's Tag property is Nothing or does not support the Icomparable Interface, Compare the .Text properties.
If the items Compare Equal and the Clicked column is not Column 0 then continue the Comparison based on the Column 0 rules above. This has the effect of using the either the source Class instances or the contents of column 0 as a secondary key for the Sort.
The result of the comparison is toggled according to if the sort is Ascending or Decending. This sort order is determined by reversing the sort order of the last click on this column.

Manages ImageLists for thumbnail display modes in the ListView control. Creates and maintains separate ImageLists for different thumbnail sizes.
Thumbnail requests are deduplicated by item path and requested size. member.remarks: The limit for capacity is ~1658 for 256px thumbnails. Viewing more images than this causes blank images to be drawn. The windows image list is stored within a contiguous section of non-virtual memory in a special region of memory which is also accessible by the gpu. The list is stored as a horizontal strip (should be vertical but isn't). Many gpus have a texture size limit of 16384px due to this being the limit for DirectX 12. Opengl supports 32768. The Nvidia 1080 has a limit of 131,072 × 65,536 but only inside cuda code. Non-cuda code is limited to 16384px. Although things still kinda work even if you exceed this limit, you will eventually start displaying blank images once you view more than 1658 thumbnails at 256px. member.name: M:ExpControlsLib.ThumbnailProvider.BytesToBitmap(System.Byte[],System.Int32)
member.summary: Converts a byte array to a of the specified size. The reason we don't store a bitmap directly in the cache is to avoid GDI handle exhaustion, as bitmaps are unmanaged resources. Instead, we store the raw pixel data and reconstruct the bitmap on demand.
member.remarks: The array must contain premultiplied-alpha BGRA pixels (i.e. produced by ImageMagick with Alpha(AlphaOption.Associate) and exported as MagickFormat.Bgra). On little-endian Windows the in-memory layout of is B, G, R, A — an exact match for BGRA bytes, so can write them directly with no channel reordering. Passing straight-alpha or non-BGRA bytes here will produce incorrect colours or transparency.
member.param: Premultiplied-alpha BGRA pixel data, 4 bytes per pixel.
The width and height of the square bitmap in pixels.
member.returns: A created from the byte array.
